title: Not vibe coding, but vibe teaching
author: drayle88
selftext:
Image honest I wanna code my own game. Have for the last 15 years. Problem: I’m mentally unable to learn coding the traditional way. I’ve spent hours trying to understand basics and I’m left with a headache and no progress. Mostly because, tutorials are 95% built a certain way, and my brain won’t grok it.

So, I’m an effort to brute force my way through this, I’ve thought about asking AI to teach me in a way I understand. 

Much like generating an image, then using it as a reference, would this method of game dev end in failure or is there possibility here?

comments.author: FreeQ1337
comments.body:
I don't think it would but hey, just try! 

Just remember failure is a process. And it will feel great when you finally tackle that bug or feature that you had no idea how to.

One day it will just click.

comments.author: bumbledog123
comments.body: I think this could work, but do you know/have examples of methods of teaching that do work for you, and what you want to learn? How much to introduce at a time? That'll be vital in this working or not

comments.author: RygaLikeTyga
comments.body: You can ask it to teach you as it helps you make your game! Ai is a really good teacher actually

comments.author: babyfern_
comments.body:
I’m majoring in game design currently and many of my professors are currently researching and testing incorporating AI in their lessons. One developed an agent to coach students through learning how to code. It’s definitely possible. You can also ask ChatGPT or Claude to create interactive learning modules as an html that you can open in your browser. 

There’s a lot of different tactics. If there’s a book you want to learn from that’s already on the internet , or a YouTube video tutorial you want help breaking down etc, give it the link and ask it to design lessons for you.

Take a learning styles quiz and give it your results, plus let it know if you need any accommodations like if you have adhd or dyslexia. It can make learning easier for you. Just make sure you tell it to use official documentation so it isn’t pulling random information from the internet.

comments.author: Frequent-Motor-492
comments.body: You could, and you probably should, but will anyone after AI truely learn to code anymore?

replies.author: drayle88
replies.body: If I was capable, I still would. I use ai to gen art, but I still draw and try to improve

replies.author: mirageofstars
replies.body: I think some people will but most won’t. Granted, AI will need to train on new code — bigger question, will there be new coding languages since no one hand codes?

replies.author: Arya_the_Gamer
replies.body: You'll still have to learn higher level programming such as algorithms and system architecture. Learning the concepts of programming such as oops, components, debugging, etc also helps a lot in the long run.

comments.author: Wavertron
comments.body:
A 4-foot tall basketballer will never play in the NBA.

It's possible you simply don't have the aptitude for coding.

I think you would be better off trying to adopt full agentic AI workflows where you never even look at the code, and just stay on the cutting edge of that as it improves. It's likely to get to the point where reading code is largely not necessary.

comments.author: Shrineheart
comments.body:
Same boat. I understand things like code structure and how it works in theory but actual implementation? I'm a mess.
So, in my case, I explain what I want the code to do. My AI will come back with additional clarifying questions. We'll go back and forth, hell write it and comment it for me so I can read over it and see what works where. I can test it, point out potential bugs sometimes fix them before he does or at least figure out where the problem is.
I'm understanding the code more because I'm learning through a passion project instead of "make this platformer" or "make this shooter" style tutorials.

comments.author: FoodTimely8137
comments.body:
That is actually a fascinating perspective, and you are definitely not alone in feeling like traditional coding tutorials just don't click with how your brain works.
​Using AI for 'vibe teaching'—where you ask it to explain concepts using analogies, game design terms, or metaphors that make sense to you rather than standard computer science syntax—can be surprisingly effective. Treating AI like a personal tutor that adapts to your learning style rather than just a code generator is a great way to break past that mental block. It won't magically write a masterpiece on day one, but using it to bridge the gap so you can finally build your game step-by-step is entirely possible. Give it a try—you might be surprised by how much further you get!

comments.author: Fuzzzy420
comments.body: Learning code is not the important part but the logic behind it. If you understand that the language you write doesn't matter and learning a different language becomes much easier.

comments.author: NebulaRisingGame
comments.body: Start with a small scope simple game.  Not the end goal game you want.  Write up as much detail on how you want it work from a player perspective, features, mechanics, etc.  Then get AI to design a plan on how to build it using best practices, security, etc.   Then get AI to explain each phase to you like your a non developer 10yr old.   Hopefully it spits out concepts you can understand and start to create a basic knowledge foundation to build off of.  Ask lots of clarifying questions and go from there.

replies.author: Brettinabox
replies.body: yea there are some pitfalls along the way and some of it has to get restructured but it works.

comments.author: Brettinabox
comments.body:

comments.author: MelvynAndrew99
comments.body: Depends on what you want to learn.  Programming, you can skip that.  Game design it will get you close but you will learn more by having people play your games and getting feedback.  So it depends on what you are looking to learn.

comments.author: lefix
comments.body: I found that biggest hurdle learning programming was how to translate all the knowledge into real projects. Like how do I go from understanding what a class or for loop is to using it to make an actual game? The answer is: by making an actual game and figuring it out step by step. You don’t wait until you have it all figured out.
